title: YRF Just Admitted the Future Isn't the Multiplex — It's Your Phone, Held Vertical
excerpt: The studio behind Pathaan, Tiger, and Alpha has invested in vertical micro-drama startup Rusk Media. And no, they won't be shrinking the Spy Universe into Reels.
body:
Here's a sentence nobody expected to read in 2026: Yash Raj Films — the studio that gave us Shah Rukh Khan running through mustard fields, the studio that built an entire spy universe across five blockbusters, the studio releasing Alpha in theatres this Thursday — has put its money into portrait-mode storytelling for teenagers.

And yet, that's exactly what happened.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=cg4Vf6PilVE

YRF announced a strategic investment in Rusk Media, a digital-first entertainment company that specialises in vertical micro-dramas and short-form animated content built for Gen Z and Gen Alpha. The financial terms weren't disclosed, but the signal is unmistakable: Bollywood's most storied production house is no longer content to live and die by the opening weekend.

Rusk Media, founded in 2019 by Mayank Yadav, operates brands like Alright! TV (fictional stories), Playground (gaming entertainment), and LIT (food, fashion, and travel) — all designed for mobile-first consumption. The startup recently raised ₹100 crore in a pre-Series C round led by Nazara Technologies, with Info Edge Ventures and IvyCap Ventures also participating. YRF's backing adds Bollywood's most powerful creative machine to what has been, until now, a purely digital-native play.

"The instinct to evolve has always been central to YRF's DNA. Platforms are infrastructure; content and IP are culture." — Akshaye Widhani, CEO, Yash Raj Films

The partnership is deliberately not about shrinking existing franchises into phone screens. There will be no vertical cut of War. No ninety-second Pathaan. Instead, the two companies will co-develop entirely original intellectual property — new stories, new characters, new worlds — conceived from the start for a portrait-orientation audience that spends more time on Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts than in a multiplex seat.

This is where the diaspora angle gets sharp.

If you're an NRI parent, you already know this: your teenager does not sit through three-hour Bollywood films. They might catch a reel of Ranveer Singh losing his mind on a press tour, but they're not blocking out an evening for Welcome To The Jungle. The generational gap in Indian cinema consumption isn't a projection — it's a fact that every family group chat on WhatsApp knows intimately. YRF is essentially building a bridge to the audience that's ageing out of event cinema before they ever aged in.

Mayank Yadav framed the ambition without pretence: "Vertical entertainment in India has produced extraordinary reach, but not the enduring IP that defines a category. That is the gap this collaboration is designed to close."

He's not wrong. Indian vertical content has produced billions of views. What it hasn't produced is a single character or franchise that sticks the way Tiger or Pathaan does. If YRF can bring franchise-building discipline to a format that runs on swipe-up attention spans, they might actually crack something no one else has.

The timing matters. YRF reported operating revenue of ₹740 crore and a net profit of ₹56 crore in FY24, according to a credit rating rationale by Acuité Ratings & Research. They're not making this move from desperation — they're making it from strength, while their theatrical slate remains the primary revenue engine. This is a hedge, not a pivot.

And they're not alone. Red Chillies, Shah Rukh Khan's production house, is also reportedly entering the micro-drama space this year. When two of Bollywood's most powerful studios independently arrive at the same conclusion — that vertical content needs serious investment — it stops being a trend and starts being an industry-wide reckoning.

The question nobody can answer yet: can a studio built on three-act structure, sweeping set pieces, and ₹300-crore budgets actually tell a story in under three minutes, on a phone, held vertical? The instinct and the ambition are right. The execution will be everything.

For now, the symbolism alone is worth noting. YRF didn't build Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge, Dhoom, or Tiger to become a digital-first company. But the fact that Akshaye Widhani's team looked at the viewing habits of the next generation and decided to meet them where they are — rather than waiting for them to come back to the cinema hall — might be the most forward-looking thing any Bollywood studio has done this decade.
